label: Slide 19
paper: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment (ASGSR 2014 poster)
heading: How much oxygen a PMMA rod needs to keep burning
shows: Each mark is one BASS-II test on a PMMA rod. The vertical axis is the final oxygen level, the horizontal axis is the stretch rate (a measure of how fast air meets the flame). Blow-off, quench, and stable-flame outcomes are marked separately.
why: Flames survive at the lowest oxygen when airflow is very slow. The authors report steady burning down to 13.6% O2 in microgravity, against 16% for the same rod in normal gravity, so a standard 1 g screening test understates the risk.
alt: Scatter plot of final oxygen concentration against stretch rate for PMMA rod tests, with blow-off, quench and stable-flame marks and a V-shaped boundary.

PSI-25.how: BASS-II’s own PMMA rod tests. Each mark is one test, with its oxygen and outcome, as in the BASS-II table.

label: Figure 11
paper: Buoyancy Effects on Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick PMMA
heading: Flame spread in normal gravity against the Saffire II result
shows: Average flame spread rate over PMMA at ambient pressures of 40 to 100 kPa in normal gravity, measured two ways. The orange point is the single Saffire II microgravity result at 100 kPa.
why: The microgravity flame spread far more slowly than the normal-gravity flame at the same pressure. Buoyant flow speeds a flame up on Earth, so ground tests do not transfer directly to orbit.
alt: Plot of average flame spread rate against pressure with two rising normal-gravity series and one low orange microgravity point.

PSI-99.how: Saffire-II’s own result (the orange point) next to ground tests at different pressures.

PSI-98.how: Saffire-II result with ground comparisons; the same fuel type (PMMA) is not in Saffire-I.

PSI-100.how: Saffire-II result with ground comparisons, for context.

label: Figure 5
paper: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity
heading: How big a droplet is when its flame goes out
shows: Droplet diameter at extinction against initial droplet diameter for more than 100 FLEX tests. Marker size shows the ambient oxygen fraction, and colour shows the diluent gas.
why: Larger droplets at lower oxygen go out soon after ignition through radiative heat loss (the paper's explanation), while smaller droplets follow a roughly straight line. The extinction size depends on both oxygen level and droplet size.
alt: Bubble plot of extinction diameter against initial droplet diameter with two trend lines.

PSI-69.how: FLEX’s own tests. The plotted quantities are the “Initial droplet diameter” and “Visible flame extinction diameter” columns of the FLEX table.

PSI-68.how: FLEX-2 repeats FLEX droplet burning; these are FLEX results.

label: Figure 4
paper: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity
heading: Cool-flame extinction size against oxygen level
shows: Droplet diameter at cool-flame extinction for n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane, plotted against ambient oxygen concentration. Panel (a) is oxygen and nitrogen only, panel (b) substitutes other diluents.
why: The extinction diameter falls as oxygen rises, so the cool flame persists to smaller droplet sizes in richer atmospheres.
alt: Two log-log panels of extinction diameter against oxygen concentration for three n-alkane fuels, each with a falling dashed trend line.

paper: Particle Morphology and Size Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-2
heading: Smoke particle size against air velocity
shows: Particle diameters measured from lampwick smoke at three air velocities, with least-squares lines through each statistic.
why: The authors find larger particles at low flow, and say smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be much larger than smoke released in ventilated areas. Detectors have to cope with that range.
alt: Plot of mean particle diameters against air velocity from 0 to 8 cm/s, with falling linear fits.

heading: Carbon monoxide made against carbon dioxide made
shows: Each point is one BASS-II test: how much CO and CO2 the burn added to the glovebox air, grouped by sample shape.
why: Concurrent-flow rods made the most CO for their CO2. The report notes the CO to CO2 ratio is well above what an efficient fire gives, so these small microgravity flames burn less completely and release more toxic CO.

heading: Oxygen used against carbon dioxide made

shows: Spread rate along black PMMA rods of three diameters, in microgravity at about 17.6 to 20.8% oxygen and in normal gravity at 19% and 21%.

heading: Oxygen level at which flames went out
shows: Oxygen at extinction against the flow speed just before extinction, for sheets of PMMA of different width and thickness. Circle size and number reflect sheet thickness.
why: Extinction happened between roughly 17 and 22% oxygen depending on flow and sample. There is no single safe oxygen number: it depends on the airflow past the fuel.

heading: Spread rate against fuel thickness
shows: Flame spread rate over PMMA from microgravity, downward-burning and other experiments, over fuel thicknesses from tens of micrometres to centimetres. Lines show the thermally thin and thermally thick limits.
why: Thin fuels spread fast and the rate falls steeply as thickness grows, then levels off for thick fuel. Fuel thickness is one of the strongest controls on how a fire spreads.

paper: BASS: An Overview of Recent ISS Results (slides)
heading: What a flammability boundary is
shows: A sketch from the BASS team: oxygen fraction against flow speed. Inside the curve a fuel can burn, outside it cannot. The red band is the buoyant flow of normal gravity.
why: The curve turns up at both high and low flow, so a fuel can be safe in a breeze and flammable in still air, or the reverse. BASS tested this at constant oxygen while changing the flow.
alt: What a flammability boundary is. A sketch from the BASS team: oxygen fraction against flow speed. Inside the curve a fuel can burn, outside it cannot. The red band is the buoyant flow of normal gravity.

paper: BASS: An Overview of Recent ISS Results (slides)
heading: Thin fuel: spread rate against flow speed
shows: Flame spread rate over thin fabric against forced flow velocity. Negative velocities are opposed flow, positive are concurrent flow (flow in the direction of spread).
why: In concurrent flow the spread rate rises roughly linearly with flow. In opposed flow it is fastest at an intermediate speed, and the flame goes out when the flow falls too low.
alt: Thin fuel: spread rate against flow speed. Flame spread rate over thin fabric against forced flow velocity. Negative velocities are opposed flow, positive are concurrent flow (flow in the direction of spread).

paper: BASS: An Overview of Recent ISS Results (slides)
heading: Nitrogen flow on a burning sphere
shows: Image grid of a PMMA sphere burning in a wake configuration in air, with a nitrogen flow switched on and then off.
why: A nitrogen flow of 500 cc/min weakened the flame but did not put it out. Suppression by inert gas needs more than a gentle flow.
alt: Nitrogen flow on a burning sphere. Image grid of a PMMA sphere burning in a wake configuration in air, with a nitrogen flow switched on and then off.

heading: Two ways a droplet flame goes out
shows: Droplet and flame size over time for n-heptane in 30 to 70% oxygen-helium at 1 atm, marked with radiative and diffusive extinction.
why: A flame can die because it loses heat by radiation (large droplet, low oxygen) or because it runs out of fuel and oxidiser supply (small droplet). FLEX measured both in space.

heading: A droplet that keeps burning after the flame seems to go out
shows: Droplet size over time for three examples of second-stage (cool flame) burning: heptane in air, and in oxygen-nitrogen and oxygen-nitrogen-carbon dioxide mixes.
why: After the visible hot flame ends, the droplet keeps shrinking, because a cool flame continues burning. This was first seen in the FLEX experiments.

paper: Cool Flames in Space, a Hot Prospect on Earth! (slides)
heading: A model that reproduces the cool flame
shows: Computed peak flame temperature over time for an n-heptane droplet (3.91 mm) in air at 1 atm, showing a hot-flame stage, then a lower-temperature cool-flame stage, then pure evaporation.
why: Models that include low-temperature chemistry capture the second stage. The slide says how well they predict extinction is still open.

heading: How a burning droplet shrinks
shows: Representative data from a microgravity droplet experiment: square of droplet diameter (left axis) and of flame diameter (right axis) against time since ignition. The figure shows droplet swelling, flame contraction and different burning-rate constants (K).
why: The droplet size squared falls along nearly straight lines, and the slope is the burning rate. This is the basic measurement FLEX-2 repeats. Data in the figure are credited in the source to Aharon and Shaw (1998).
alt: How a burning droplet shrinks. Representative data from a microgravity droplet experiment: square of droplet diameter (left axis) and of flame diameter (right axis) against time since ignition. The figure shows droplet swelling, flame contraction and different burning-rate constants (K).

heading: Burning rate against starting droplet size
shows: Measured burning rate against initial droplet diameter, with three model lines: no radiation, non-luminous radiation, and soot radiation. Points come from drop-tower tests.
why: The model that includes radiation from soot tracks the measured fall in burning rate for larger droplets. This is the kind of comparison FLEX-2 was designed to extend in space.

shows: Droplet diameter when the cool flame went out, for n-dodecane in 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen, against pressure. Triangles are droplets held on a fibre, circles are free floating.

heading: Does swapping helium for nitrogen change it?
shows: The same measurement for four atmospheres: 17% O2 in nitrogen, 21% O2 in nitrogen, and 21% O2 with helium in place of some nitrogen.
why: Helium-rich mixes show cool-flame extinction at pressures where the nitrogen mixes show none, so the gas that dilutes the oxygen matters as well as the oxygen level.

shows: Images of an n-butane flame at test point 21174C3: (a) hot flame, (b) cool flame. The dashed circle marks the gas-fed porous sphere burner, and colours are added from grayscale.
why: The cool flame is dimmer and has a different structure. CFI-G was built to find where cool flames exist as oxygen and fuel mix change.

heading: Heat needed to gasify the fuel, in space and on Earth
shows: Preliminary flammability map from the burning-rate emulator: heat of gasification against fuel mixture mass flux, microgravity data against normal-gravity data, each with a fitted line.
why: The microgravity points sit well below the normal-gravity line, so the burner flames behave differently without buoyancy. This is the quantity needed to relate a gas burner to a burning solid.
alt: Heat needed to gasify the fuel, in space and on Earth. Preliminary flammability map from the burning-rate emulator: heat of gasification against fuel mixture mass flux, microgravity data against normal-gravity data, each with a fitted line.

heading: How much of the flame heat is radiated
shows: Flame radiant fraction against fuel mixture mass flux (a) and flame height (b) for the steady tests.
why: The radiant fraction rises with flame height. A larger share of radiation means more heat reaches the surroundings, which is what ignites nearby materials.
alt: How much of the flame heat is radiated. Flame radiant fraction against fuel mixture mass flux (a) and flame height (b) for the steady tests.

PSI-20.how: BRE’s own tests. Radiant fraction is not in the BRE table, so this figure is where that result is.

heading: Electric current through a flame
shows: Ion current against field strength for a methane jet at 15 cm/s (left) and 19 cm/s (right), with no coflow.
why: The current rises to a peak near 1.4 to 1.5 kV/cm and then falls and levels off. It is how the experiment measures the way a flame responds to an electric field.
alt: Electric current through a flame. Ion current against field strength for a methane jet at 15 cm/s (left) and 19 cm/s (right), with no coflow.

heading: Flame shape as the field is raised, with coflow
shows: Flame images at field strengths from 0.06 to 2.00 kV/cm with a 3.1 cm/s coflow, for two methane jet speeds.
why: The yellow soot glow at the flame tip fades and the flame changes shape as the field grows, so an electric field can be used to steer how much soot a flame makes.

shows: Flames from four tests (GMT 013) in which the hydrogen and methane fuel flow rises from left to right while the nitrogen flow stays constant, in about 19% oxygen at about 1 atm.

shows: Three s-Flame tests of methane (45%) burning in 30% oxygen, with the fuel flow changing between tests.

heading: How long a flame is when it starts to smoke
shows: Smoke point flame length against coflow velocity for several fuels and burner sizes (0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm).
why: The longer the flame can get before it smokes, the less sooty the fuel. Coflow speed changes the smoke point, and the fuels separate clearly.

heading: One line through many fuels
shows: Smoke point length against fuel mass flow divided by the stoichiometric mixture fraction, for all the fuels and burners. A straight line through the origin is fitted (y = 1.6097x, R2 = 0.9514).
why: When the flow is scaled this way, the many fuels fall on one line, a simple rule for predicting smoke point length.
alt: One line through many fuels. Smoke point length against fuel mass flow divided by the stoichiometric mixture fraction, for all the fuels and burners. A straight line through the origin is fitted (y = 1.6097x, R2 = 0.9514).

heading: Flames at four coflow speeds
shows: Photographs of a 75% propylene flame from a 1.6 mm burner at coflow speeds of 28.2, 32.9, 37.6 and 42.3 cm/s.

heading: The same smoke, four different detectors
shows: Normalised mass concentration needed for an alarm, against smoke particle size, for four smoke detector technologies. The alarm level was set at 2 mg/m3 for 500 nm particles.
why: Particle counters and two other designs need very different smoke amounts as particles get bigger, while a scattering detector stays flat. Detector choice depends on the particle size a fire makes in space.

shows: Simulated smoke distribution 177 s after a smoke source of 8.5 mg/s was switched on at location 4 on the floor of an enclosure with obstructions.
why: Smoke takes time to reach a detector and obstructions change how long it takes. Detector placement matters as much as detector type.

heading: Simulated smoke plumes, four cases
shows: Visualisation of simulated smoke fields for four cases (1MG, 1EG, 2MG, 2EG) behind a bluff body.
why: Without gravity the plume spreads evenly behind the body, while the gravity cases rise. The same smoke is easier or harder to detect depending on where it goes.
alt: Simulated smoke plumes, four cases. Visualisation of simulated smoke fields for four cases (1MG, 1EG, 2MG, 2EG) behind a bluff body.

PSI-115.how: The report behind this record’s simulation files: smoke fields for the same cases.

paper: Dissertation: Combustion Behavior of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated and N-Alkane Droplets
heading: Modelled methanol droplet at different oxygen levels
shows: Predicted droplet size, peak gas temperature and flame stand-off ratio over time for methanol droplets of 1 mm (top) and 2 mm (bottom) in 7%, 10% and 21% oxygen at 1 atm.
why: Less oxygen shortens the burn and lowers the peak temperature. These model results are not measurements.
alt: Modelled methanol droplet at different oxygen levels. Predicted droplet size, peak gas temperature and flame stand-off ratio over time for methanol droplets of 1 mm (top) and 2 mm (bottom) in 7%, 10% and 21% oxygen at 1 atm.

PSI-117.how: The dissertation hosted on this record. These model results use the same kind of droplets as the FLEX data it analyses.

paper: Dissertation: Combustion Behavior of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated and N-Alkane Droplets
heading: Flame stand-off for an n-butanol droplet
shows: Flame stand-off ratio (flame diameter over droplet diameter) against time, measured and predicted, for a 0.56 mm n-butanol droplet in air.
why: The stand-off ratio grows as the droplet shrinks, and the model follows the measurement closely until the flame goes out.
alt: Flame stand-off for an n-butanol droplet. Flame stand-off ratio (flame diameter over droplet diameter) against time, measured and predicted, for a 0.56 mm n-butanol droplet in air.

PSI-117.how: The dissertation hosted on this record. Model against measurement for a droplet like those in the FLEX tests it analyses.

paper: Dissertation: Combustion Behavior of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated and N-Alkane Droplets
heading: Adding ozone to a droplet flame
shows: Predicted droplet size and peak gas temperature for n-heptane droplets with 1 to 7% ozone added, for 0.1 mm and 0.5 mm droplets.
why: Ozone speeds up ignition and changes the cool-flame stage. This is a model result for tiny droplets, not a measurement.
alt: Adding ozone to a droplet flame. Predicted droplet size and peak gas temperature for n-heptane droplets with 1 to 7% ozone added, for 0.1 mm and 0.5 mm droplets.

PSI-117.how: The dissertation hosted on this record. A model result for the ozone effect, not a measurement.

paper: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (slides)
heading: Saffire-I: flame spread over fabric
shows: Left: flame base and pyrolysis front position over time, in concurrent and opposed flow. Right: spread rate against air flow speed for fabric samples of two widths.
why: This is the first large (40 cm by 94 cm) fabric fire burned in space. Concurrent-flow flames spread faster as flow rose, and quenched at low flow.
alt: Saffire-I: flame spread over fabric. Left: flame base and pyrolysis front position over time, in concurrent and opposed flow. Right: spread rate against air flow speed for fabric samples of two widths.

PSI-100.how: Saffire-III reuses the Saffire design; this is the Saffire-I fabric result.

why: Oxygen was one of the module's own measurements of the fire. The axis values are small at this size, so open the slides for the detail.

why: The flame grew slowly and steadily across the sample over several minutes, a pattern that small tests cannot reproduce.

paper: An Experimental and Computational Study on Soot Formation in a Coflow Jet Flame Under Microgravity
heading: Soot in a flame with and without gravity
shows: Measured soot temperature and soot volume fraction for matching methane flames in normal gravity and microgravity, with computed results.
why: The microgravity flame is wider and taller, produces about eight times more peak soot, and runs about 200 K cooler than the normal-gravity flame.
alt: Soot in a flame with and without gravity. Measured soot temperature and soot volume fraction for matching methane flames in normal gravity and microgravity, with computed results.
